title: Mock 2 · Ecosystem & Structures
blurb: Who's who in a Category III AIF, how funds are structured and launched, plus first-step performance metrics.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly excluded from the definition of an Alternative Investment Fund under the SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012?
options: A privately pooled hedge fund registered with SEBI
A family trust set up for the benefit of a family
A venture capital fund investing in start-ups
A private equity fund investing in unlisted companies
questions.explanation: The AIF definition excludes mutual funds, collective investment schemes, family trusts, ESOP or employee benefit trusts, holding companies, securitisation SPVs and funds regulated by RBI or other regulators.
hints: A SEBI-registered privately pooled hedge fund is a Category III AIF.
Correct: family trusts, ESOP trusts and holding companies are excluded.
VCFs are Category I AIFs.
PE funds are Category II AIFs.

questions.q: An Angel Fund must on-board at least how many accredited investors before declaring its first close?
options: Two
Five
Ten
Twenty-five
questions.explanation: An Angel Fund (sub-category of Category I) shall on-board at least five accredited investors before declaring its first close. Its investment in any investee company must be between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 25 crore.
hints: Two is too few under the 2025 amendment.
Correct: at least five accredited investors before first close.
Ten is not the prescribed number.
Twenty-five is not the requirement.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of investors permitted in a single scheme of a Category III AIF?
options: No upper limit
questions.explanation: Every scheme launched by a Category III AIF shall have a maximum of 1,000 investors, and this is checked in the Compliance Test Report.
hints: 200 relates to private placement rules elsewhere, not this limit.
Correct: each scheme can have a maximum of 1,000 investors.
500 is not the AIF limit.
Unlimited investors apply to mutual funds, not AIFs.

questions.q: A 'PIPE' fund operating as a Category III AIF typically:
options: Invests only in unlisted start-ups
Buys securities of a publicly traded company at a discount to its current market price
Lends money to infrastructure projects
Invests exclusively in units of other AIFs
questions.explanation: PIPE (Private Investment in Public Equity) funds purchase securities of a publicly traded stock at a discount to the current market price, in the primary or secondary market.
hints: Unlisted start-ups are the domain of VCFs.
Correct: PIPE = Private Investment in Public Equity, usually at a discount.
Infrastructure lending suits infrastructure or debt funds.
That describes a fund of funds approach.

questions.q: Why do investment managers prefer a high catch-up rate in the contribution agreement?
options: Because it reduces the hurdle rate payable to investors
Because a higher proportion of residual profits after capital and hurdle flows to the manager until it reaches its agreed profit share
Because it allows the manager to skip returning investors' capital first
Because it lowers the GST payable on management fees
questions.explanation: Catch-up rate is the rate at which residual profits, after returning capital and hurdle, are paid to the manager until it receives its pre-determined share of total profits. With a 100% catch-up, all residual profits go to the manager until that share is met.
hints: The hurdle remains payable first; catch-up comes after it.
Correct: catch-up accelerates the manager's share of profits after the hurdle is paid.
Return of capital is always the first step of the waterfall.
Catch-up has nothing to do with GST.

questions.q: In a master-feeder structure for a Category III AIF, where is the management fee typically charged?
options: At the master fund level, with only a symbolic fixed amount charged at the feeder level
Only at the feeder fund level
Equally at both the master and feeder levels
Directly to the investee companies
questions.explanation: In a master-feeder structure, management fees are typically charged at the master fund level, while the feeder charges a symbolic fixed absolute amount (for example USD 1,000). The master's fee is passed to feeder managers through the NAV allocated to the feeder.
hints: Correct: fees are charged at the master; feeders charge a token amount such as USD 1,000.
Feeders charge only a symbolic amount, not the main fee.
Double charging is what the structure avoids.
Investee companies do not pay the fund's management fee.

questions.q: Why is the appointment of a Registrar and Transfer Agent (RTA) compulsory for a Category III AIF?
options: RTAs act as collecting agents for stamp duty on issue, transfer and sale of AIF units
RTAs file the PPM with SEBI
RTAs hold the fund's securities in safekeeping
RTAs value the fund's unlisted investments
questions.explanation: After the Indian Stamp Act amendments, RTAs registered with SEBI act as collecting agents to collect stamp duty on issue, transfer and sale of AIF units; hence appointment of an RTA by a Category III AIF is compulsory.
hints: Correct: SEBI made RTAs collecting agents for stamp duty, so appointment is compulsory.
PPM filing is done through a merchant banker.
Safekeeping is the custodian's job.
Valuation of unlisted securities is done by an independent valuer.

questions.q: If a Category III AIF wishes to change its investment strategy during the life of the fund, whose approval is required?
options: At least 75% of the investors by number
Only the trustee of the fund
At least two-thirds of the investors by value of their investment
A simple majority of investors by number
questions.explanation: The investment strategy disclosed in the PPM applies for the fund life. Any change requires approval of at least two-thirds of investors by value of their investment in the Category III AIF.
hints: 75% applies to other matters such as associate transactions and winding up, and it is by value.
Trustee approval alone is not sufficient.
Correct: a change in investment strategy needs approval of two-thirds of investors by value.
A simple majority by number is not the test.

questions.q: An individual has met the accredited investor criteria in each of the two preceding financial years. For how long will the accreditation be valid?
options: 1 year from the date of accreditation
2 years from the date of accreditation
3 years from the date of accreditation
5 years from the date of accreditation
questions.explanation: Accreditation is valid for 2 years if the applicant meets the criteria for the preceding one year, and for 3 years if the criteria are met in each of the two preceding financial years.
hints: 1 year is not a validity period under the framework.
2 years applies when criteria are met only for the preceding one year.
Correct: consistent eligibility in both preceding FYs earns 3-year validity.
5 years is not provided for.

questions.q: A Category III AIF has called-up capital of Rs 100 crore and a compounding hurdle rate of 8% p.a. What is the reference hurdle at the end of Year 2?
options: Rs 116.00 crore
Rs 108.00 crore
Rs 116.64 crore
Rs 125.97 crore
questions.explanation: The reference hurdle is computed by applying the hurdle rate to the previous reference hurdle: Year 1 = 100 x 1.08 = 108; Year 2 = 108 x 1.08 = 116.64 crore.
hints: This is simple interest (100 + 2 x 8); the workbook compounds the hurdle.
This is the Year 1 reference hurdle.
This is the Year 3 reference hurdle (100 x 1.08^3).

questions.q: A fund has paid-in capital of Rs 200 crore, has distributed Rs 80 crore and holds unrealised investments valued at Rs 260 crore. What is its TVPI?
hints: 0.40 is the DPI only.
1.30 is the RVPI only.
This wrongly divides 420 by 200 after double counting.
Correct: DPI 0.40 + RVPI 1.30 = TVPI 1.70.

questions.q: The Treynor ratio measures excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of:
options: Systematic risk, measured by beta
Total risk, measured by standard deviation
Maximum drawdown
Value at Risk
questions.explanation: Treynor ratio = (Rp - Rf) / beta. It compares the risk premium with non-diversifiable (systematic) risk, whereas the Sharpe ratio uses total risk.
hints: Correct: Treynor divides the risk premium by beta.
Standard deviation is used by the Sharpe ratio.
Maximum drawdown is a separate risk metric.
VaR is a downside-loss measure, not Treynor's denominator.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Gross IRR and Net IRR of a Category III AIF is correct?
options: Gross IRR is always lower than Net IRR
Net IRR ignores management and incentive fees
Net IRR is computed at investor level after fees, expenses and taxes and is lower than Gross IRR
Gross IRR is computed after deducting taxes paid by the fund
questions.explanation: Gross IRR uses fund-level flows before management fees, incentive fees, expenses and taxes. Net IRR uses investor-level flows including these costs, so it is lower than Gross IRR.
hints: Gross IRR excludes costs, so it is higher, not lower.
Net IRR specifically includes these fees as outflows.
Correct: net IRR treats fund expenses as borne by investors, so it is lower.
Gross IRR is before fees, expenses and taxes.

questions.q: What is the target portfolio beta of a Category III AIF following a market-neutral strategy?
options: Exactly 1
Above 2
Zero or close to zero
Equal to the beta of the benchmark index
questions.explanation: Market-neutral funds take equal long and short exposures so that the fund is neutral to the broad market; the portfolio beta is zero or close to zero.
hints: Beta of 1 means the fund moves with the market.
High beta implies higher volatility, the opposite of neutrality.
Correct: market-neutral funds aim for beta near zero.
Matching the index beta would make the fund track the market.

questions.q: The collapse of Long Term Capital Management (LTCM) in 1998 is cited in the workbook mainly to highlight which due diligence concern?
options: The danger of investing only in listed equities
The need for a minimum corpus of Rs 20 crore
The risk of high exit loads
The danger of excessive leverage in the fund's strategy
questions.explanation: LTCM had about USD 5 billion equity and over USD 125 billion borrowings (leverage of about 30:1). Losses after the 1998 Russian default were magnified by leverage, so investors should scrutinise leverage in due diligence.
hints: LTCM traded sovereign bond convergence, not listed equities alone.
Minimum corpus is an Indian rule unrelated to LTCM.
Exit loads were not the cause of LTCM's failure.
Correct: LTCM ran about 30:1 leverage and collapsed after the Russian default.

questions.q: An independent valuer appointed by a Category III AIF must have at least how many years of experience in valuation of unlisted securities?
options: 1 year
5 years
3 years
10 years
questions.explanation: The independent valuer must not be an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee, must have at least 3 years of experience in valuing unlisted securities, and must meet the IBBI/professional membership or rating-agency criteria.
hints: 1 year is insufficient under the eligibility criteria.
5 years is not the prescribed minimum.
Correct: at least 3 years of experience is required.
10 years is not prescribed.

questions.q: A Category III AIF buys 100 lots of a stock futures contract with a lot size of 50 shares at a futures price of Rs 2,000. What is the notional exposure taken?
questions.explanation: Futures exposure = number of lots x lot size x futures price = 100 x 50 x Rs 2,000 = Rs 1,00,00,000.
hints: This misses a factor of 10.
This multiplies only lots and price.
This multiplies only lots, lot size and Rs 20.
Correct: 100 x 50 x 2,000 = Rs 1 crore.

questions.q: For listed equity shares sold by a Category III AIF after more than 12 months with STT paid, long-term capital gains are taxed at:
options: 20% on the entire gain
10% on gains exceeding Rs 1 lakh
30% at the maximum marginal rate
12.5% on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh in a financial year
questions.explanation: Table 9.1 of the workbook: long-term capital gains on listed equity shares and equity-oriented units (STT paid) are taxed at 12.5% on the amount exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh in a financial year.
hints: 20% is the STCG rate for listed equity.
10% above Rs 1 lakh is the old regime, not the 2026 workbook rule.
MMR applies to business income, not STT-paid LTCG.
Correct: the post-July 23, 2024 rate is 12.5% above Rs 1.25 lakh.

questions.q: Why does GST paid on management fees become an extra cost for a domestic Category III AIF?
options: The fund has no output GST liability, so it cannot use input tax credit for GST paid
GST on management fees is charged at 28%
GST is payable twice, by the fund and by each investor
GST is charged on the fund's capital gains
questions.explanation: GST is levied on management fees, trusteeship fees and services of external providers. As a pooled vehicle the fund has no output GST liability, so it cannot benefit from input tax credit, making GST an incremental cost indirectly borne by investors.
hints: Correct: with no output GST, the input credit is wasted and investors bear the cost.
The workbook uses 18% GST on management fees.
There is no double levy on fund and investors for the same fee.
GST applies to services such as fees, not to capital gains.

questions.q: According to the workbook, what are the four pillars of AIF distributorship?
options: Marketing, Sales, Investor Support and Relationship Management
Research, Trading, Settlement and Custody
Valuation, Audit, Compliance and Taxation
Sourcing, Structuring, Monitoring and Exit
questions.explanation: Marketing, Sales, Investor Support and Relationship Management form the four pillars of AIF distributorship, supporting long-term engagement with managers and investors.
hints: Correct: these are the four pillars named in the workbook.
These are investment operations functions, not distribution pillars.
These are fund governance functions.
These describe a private equity deal cycle.

questions.q: Professional Indemnity (Errors and Omissions) insurance bought by a Category III AIF primarily protects:
options: The Category III AIF against costs arising from losses caused to investors by errors or omissions in its services
Directors personally against all claims including fraud
Investors against market losses in any bad year
The distributor against loss of commission
questions.explanation: Professional Indemnity (E&O) insurance protects the Category III AIF from costs borne as a result of substantial losses caused to an investor due to errors and omissions in its services.
hints: Correct: E&O protects the fund that bought the policy.
D&O protects directors, and even it excludes fraud.
No insurance covers ordinary market losses.
Distributor commissions are not covered by this policy.

questions.q: Which fund structure meets Zenith's goal of pooling Indian HNIs and the Singapore fund in one onshore vehicle?
options: Parallel structure
Offshore fund structure
Master-feeder structure with no onshore pooling
Unified structure
questions.explanation: In a unified structure, commitments from domestic and offshore investors are pooled into one onshore AIF, letting the India-based team earn management and performance fees for the whole structure. No FIPB approval is needed; the automatic route applies.
hints: In a parallel structure, offshore funds invest directly alongside, not into, the onshore AIF.
A pure offshore structure has no pooling in India.
Without onshore pooling, the Indian team would not earn all fees at one level.
Correct: a unified structure pools domestic and offshore commitments in an onshore AIF.
questions.case: Zenith Asset Managers applied to SEBI on 10 February 2026 to register 'Zenith Long-Short Fund' as a Category III AIF set up as a trust. SEBI granted registration on 1 March 2026. The first scheme is a close-ended scheme with a target corpus of Rs 400 crore and a tenure of 5 years. Zenith wants Indian HNIs and a Singapore-based fund to invest in the same Indian (onshore) pooling vehicle so that the Indian team earns all fees at one level. Later, it files the PPM of a second scheme with SEBI through a merchant banker on 1 June 2026.

questions.q: From which date can Zenith launch its first scheme?
options: 10 February 2026, the date of application
1 March 2026, being the later of the registration date and 10 working days after filing
24 February 2026, ten working days after filing
1 June 2026, when the second PPM is filed
questions.explanation: First schemes of an AIF can be launched from the date of grant of SEBI registration or after 10 working days of filing the application, whichever is later. Registration on 1 March 2026 is later, so that is the launch date.
hints: The fund cannot launch before SEBI grants registration.
Correct: the first scheme can launch from the later of the two dates, which is the registration date here.
Ten working days had passed, but registration came later, so the later date applies.
The second scheme's filing is unrelated to the first scheme's launch.
questions.case: Zenith Asset Managers applied to SEBI on 10 February 2026 to register 'Zenith Long-Short Fund' as a Category III AIF set up as a trust. SEBI granted registration on 1 March 2026. Zenith wants Indian HNIs and a Singapore-based fund to invest in the same Indian (onshore) pooling vehicle so that the Indian team earns all fees at one level. Later, it files the PPM of a second scheme with SEBI through a merchant banker on 1 June 2026.

questions.q: From which date will the 5-year tenure of the first close-ended scheme be computed?
options: From the date of SEBI registration
From the date of final close
From the date of the first investment by the fund
From the date of the first close of the scheme
questions.explanation: For close-ended Category III AIFs the tenure is determined at registration and computed from the date of first close of the scheme.
hints: Registration does not start the tenure clock.
Final close is later; tenure starts at first close.
The first investment date is not the reference point.
Correct: tenure is computed from the date of first close.
questions.case: Zenith Asset Managers applied to SEBI on 10 February 2026 to register 'Zenith Long-Short Fund' as a Category III AIF set up as a trust. SEBI granted registration on 1 March 2026. The first scheme is a close-ended scheme with a target corpus of Rs 400 crore and a tenure of 5 years. Zenith wants Indian HNIs and a Singapore-based fund to invest in the same Indian (onshore) pooling vehicle so that the Indian team earns all fees at one level. Later, it files the PPM of a second scheme with SEBI through a merchant banker on 1 June 2026.

questions.q: Under the regular-scheme route, when can Zenith launch the second scheme whose PPM was filed through a merchant banker on 1 June 2026?
options: After 10 working days of filing the PPM with SEBI
Immediately on filing the PPM
Only after SEBI formally approves the PPM
After 30 working days of filing the PPM
questions.explanation: Under the GARUDA framework, regular schemes file the PPM through a merchant banker at least 10 working days before launch, and new schemes can be launched after 10 working days of filing. SEBI does not approve the PPM.
hints: Correct: new regular schemes can launch after 10 working days of filing.
Immediate launch on filing is available to AI-only funds and LVFs, not regular schemes.
SEBI only gives observations; it does not approve PPMs.
30 days was the older timeline, replaced by 10 working days in 2026.
